connection: Session 14 created a constrained SelectGreater<T> method in its own ScratchPad class. Preserve that completed experiment and create a Session 15 copy whose constraint can be removed temporarily without damaging earlier work.
objectives: Explain what where T : IComparable<T> promises the compiler about any type T used to call SelectGreater<T>.
Remove the constraint experimentally and read the exact compile error left.CompareTo(right) produces without it.
Explain why Employee cannot be passed to SelectGreater<T> today, and what Employee would need to implement to become usable there.

Distinguish a constraint that restricts which types are allowed (where T : IComparable<T>) from one that guarantees a default constructor (where T : new()) -- neither of which this codebase currently needs the second kind of.

visuals.title: A constraint is a promise the caller must keep
visuals.explanation: where T : IComparable<T> tells the compiler: whatever T ends up being, it will have a CompareTo method -- SelectGreater<T>'s body is only allowed to compile because of that promise.

visuals.title: Without the constraint, CompareTo is not guaranteed to exist
visuals.explanation: Remove where T : IComparable<T> and left.CompareTo(right) stops compiling -- the compiler no longer knows T has a CompareTo method at all.

visuals.title: DateTime and int qualify; Employee does not
visuals.explanation: System.DateTime and System.Int32 both implement IComparable<T> in the .NET base class library. Employee implements no such interface.

visuals.title: Constraints select a category of types, not one type
visuals.explanation: where T : IComparable<T> does not name DateTime or int specifically -- it opens SelectGreater<T> to any type, present or future, that satisfies the same promise.

preQuiz.prompt: What does where T : IComparable<T> actually guarantee inside SelectGreater<T>'s method body?
options: That left.CompareTo(right) is a valid call, because every T the method could be instantiated with is guaranteed to implement IComparable<T>
That T must be a value type
That T has a public parameterless constructor
preQuiz.explanation: A type constraint's entire purpose is unlocking specific members (here, CompareTo) inside the generic method body -- without it, the compiler assumes nothing about T beyond 'it is some type.'

preQuiz.prompt: If you remove where T : IComparable<T> from SelectGreater<T>, what specifically fails to compile?
options: left.CompareTo(right) -- the compiler no longer knows CompareTo exists on an unconstrained T
Nothing -- the method still compiles and works identically
preQuiz.explanation: The method's own body is what breaks -- this is the direct, observable consequence of removing a constraint the body actually relies on.

preQuiz.prompt: Why can't SelectGreater<Employee> be called with two real Employee objects today?
options: Employee implements no comparison interface (no IComparable<Employee>) -- there is no defined ordering between two employees for CompareTo to express
preQuiz.explanation: This is not a limitation of generics -- it is a real, honest gap: nobody has defined what it would mean for one Employee to be 'greater than' another, so the language correctly refuses to guess.

concept.title: The constraint unlocks CompareTo inside the method body
paragraphs: Without where T : IComparable<T>, the compiler treats an unconstrained T as offering nothing beyond object's own members (ToString, Equals, GetHashCode) -- CompareTo is not among them.
Adding the constraint is what makes left.CompareTo(right) a legal call: the compiler now knows, for certain, that whatever concrete type T turns out to be, it will have that method.

concept.title: DateTime and int qualify; Employee does not -- and that's correct
paragraphs: System.DateTime implements IComparable<DateTime>; System.Int32 (what int aliases) implements IComparable<Int32>. Both were designed with a natural ordering (earlier/later, smaller/larger).

Employee has no such natural ordering defined anywhere in the production code -- and inventing one (by EmployeeId? by Name alphabetically?) would be a real design decision, not something to guess at inside this session.

concept.title: Other constraint kinds this codebase does not currently need
paragraphs: where T : class restricts T to reference types; where T : struct restricts to value types; where T : new() requires a public parameterless constructor. None of SelectGreater<T>'s callers need any of these -- IComparable<T> is the only constraint this codebase's generic code actually requires.
Naming these honestly as unused, rather than forcing a contrived example, keeps this session's claims accurate to the real code.
concept.code:
// Not used anywhere in this codebase -- shown for contrast only

lab.objective: Prove what a generic constraint does by building a valid constrained method, temporarily removing its promise, and observing failures in both the method body and an invalid caller.
lab.startingCondition: Session 14's completed class already contains a valid SelectGreater<T>. Keep it unchanged; create a Session 15 ScratchPad class so intentional compiler failures remain isolated to this session.
steps: Open the ScratchPad project.
Create a Session15 folder in the ScratchPad project.
Create Session15ConstraintDemo.cs inside the new folder.
Declare a public sealed Session15ConstraintDemo class.

steps.text: Stub Run using the established session-specific ScratchPad pattern.
Stub a private static SelectGreater<T> method with the IComparable<T> constraint. The method is repeated here deliberately so you can break Session 15 without editing the completed Session 14 class.

steps: Replace the throw in SelectGreater with a local comparison variable assigned from left.CompareTo(right).
Return left when comparison is zero or positive.
Return right when comparison is negative.

steps.text: Build the valid constrained method before running either compiler experiment.

steps: Temporarily comment out only the where T : IComparable<T> line.
Build and read the compiler error on left.CompareTo(right).
Explain the error in one sentence: without the constraint, the compiler cannot promise that an arbitrary T has CompareTo.
Restore the constraint.
Build again and confirm that the method body compiles.
Replace the throw in Run by creating two integer values.
Call SelectGreater with the two integers and display the selected value.
Create two Employee objects with different IDs, names, and valid Address objects.
Predict whether SelectGreater(firstEmployee, secondEmployee) will compile.
Type that Employee call and observe the constraint error at the call site.
Explain why the compiler cannot guess whether employees should be ordered by ID, name, or another business rule.
Comment out only the invalid Employee call.
Open ScratchPad/Program.cs.
Keep every earlier session construction and Run call unchanged.
Construct one Session15ConstraintDemo object at the end of Program.cs.
Call Run on the Session15ConstraintDemo object.

postQuiz.prompt: If Employee later implemented IComparable<Employee> (say, comparing by EmployeeId), would SelectGreater<T> need any code changes to accept Employee arguments?
options: No -- SelectGreater<T>'s existing where T : IComparable<T> constraint would already accept any type that implements that interface, including a newly-comparable Employee
Yes -- a new SelectGreaterEmployee overload would need to be written
No -- but only after adding a second SelectGreater method
postQuiz.explanation: This is the real payoff of constraining by interface rather than by concrete type: any future type that satisfies IComparable<T> becomes usable with SelectGreater<T> automatically, with zero changes to SelectGreater<T> itself.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does the compiler reject SelectGreater(employeeA, employeeB) at compile time instead of, say, throwing an exception at runtime?
options: Generic constraints are checked at compile time -- the whole point is catching a type that cannot satisfy the constraint before the program ever runs, not after
It doesn't reject it -- Employee comparisons silently return an arbitrary result
Constraints are only checked in Debug builds
postQuiz.explanation: Compile-time constraint checking is exactly why generics with constraints are safer than, say, casting to object and hoping a CompareTo-like method exists at runtime.

postQuiz.prompt: What is the practical difference between SelectGreater<T>'s IComparable<T> constraint and an unconstrained generic method that just returns object?
options: The IComparable<T> constraint lets SelectGreater<T> call a real, type-safe CompareTo and return the SAME type T that was passed in; an unconstrained method returning object would lose type information and gain no safe way to compare its arguments
An unconstrained method would run faster
postQuiz.explanation: Constraints let generic code both stay safely typed AND access members specific to the constraint -- losing the constraint would cost both capabilities at once.

reflections: Why is 'Employee cannot be compared yet' a more honest lesson outcome than inventing an arbitrary ordering just to make an example work?
What real-world ordering, if any, would make sense for comparing two Employee objects, and who should decide that -- this session, or a future design decision?
How does seeing the actual compiler error (not just reading about it) change your confidence in explaining what a constraint does?
whatBreaks: Removing where T : IComparable<T> from SelectGreater<T> breaks the method's own body at the exact line that calls CompareTo -- not its callers, and not at runtime, but the method definition itself fails to compile. Attempting to call SelectGreater with two Employee arguments today fails to compile for a different, equally real reason: Employee genuinely does not implement IComparable<Employee>, and no code in this course invents a fake ordering to work around that honestly.
summary: where T : IComparable<T> is not decoration -- removing it breaks SelectGreater<T>'s own method body, because the compiler can no longer assume CompareTo exists on an unconstrained T. DateTime and int satisfy the constraint because .NET defines a natural ordering for both; Employee does not, and this session treats that as a real, currently-true fact about the codebase rather than working around it.
